Chapter 4: Talking About Race and Difference With Children
Picture this: a group of kids gathers on the playground, picking teams for a game. As they choose sides, you start to notice little patterns—sometimes it’s about who’s friends with whom, but other times, it’s about differences you might not expect.
If you’re watching from a distance, you might hope that kids just don’t notice race or ethnicity—that maybe they’re “colorblind” to all of that. The instinct is to avoid the topic, to just let kids sort it out on their own. But here’s the thing: children notice differences way earlier than most adults think.
By the time they’re in preschool, they’re already sorting and categorizing, trying to figure out the world around them. And when adults stay quiet about race, kids start filling in the gaps with their own ideas—sometimes coming to conclusions that are only half-right or just plain off-base.
Take one family for example. The parents really prided themselves on being open-minded. They never talked about race, thinking that silence would help their child be more accepting. But before long, their child started asking questions—like, “Why do some people look different?” or, “Why aren’t there more kids like me in my class?” Suddenly, those parents found themselves scrambling for answers.
Here’s something to really pay attention to: research says that avoiding conversations about race doesn’t stop bias from forming. In fact, it can make it worse. If kids don’t hear adults talk openly about these things, they might start to believe that differences are something you’re not supposed to mention—or, even worse, that some groups are better or worse than others. Without real conversation, stereotypes find a place to grow.
There was this classroom experiment where teachers tried to encourage diversity by putting up posters and reading multicultural books. Sounds good, right? But nothing really changed until the teachers actually talked with the kids—naming differences, sharing stories, and answering the tough questions. That’s when you started to see attitudes shift.
So why don’t more adults do this? Well, it’s uncomfortable. Lots of folks worry about saying the wrong thing or making matters worse. But kids need our help to really understand and appreciate diversity. They need the words to talk about what they see, and the reassurance that it’s okay to be curious.
I remember one parent who, after years of avoiding the topic, finally decided to bring it up over dinner. They just asked their child what they noticed about their classmates. It was awkward at first—nobody really knew what to say. But slowly, they found the words for their thoughts and feelings. That conversation didn’t solve everything, but it opened up a whole new way to connect.
So, here’s the key takeaway: silence isn’t neutral. Kids are already learning about race from the world around them. What they really need is for adults to help them make sense of it all. Honest, age-appropriate conversations aren’t just helpful—they build understanding, empathy, and respect. In a world full of differences, talking openly is one of the best ways we can show we care.
